item.title: Magenta solar panels may be agrivoltaics' cleverest trick yet
item.description:
Vegetable farms and solar farms both need lots of sunlight and open space. But how do we divide our limited lands between these two priorities? One elegant solution is to put crops and solar panels on the same land—and share the broad spectrum of incoming sunlight between them.

A new study in Cell Reports Physical Science does this with photovoltaic cells that are semi-transparent: They capture some wavelengths of sunlight to make electricity, while letting the wavelengths most critical to photosynthesis pass through and reach the plants below. The new study suggests that broccoli can be grown in the magenta shade of these solar panels—without sacrificing the harvest.

Agrivoltaic schemes—putting plants and solar on the same land – could help us avoid clearing more land for human use. Climate studies suggest that this might work especially well across a wide sunbathed swath of the United States, from Texas up to Nebraska and west to California. Devoting just one percent of U.S. farmland to agrivoltaics could cover up to 20 percent of the nation’s electricity needs.

But traditional photovoltaic panels are opaque—and by shading plants, they can reduce crop yields. So engineers are trying to create new photovoltaic cells that divide the spectrum of sunlight between plants and electricity generation—similar to how governments segment different frequency bands for television, radio, cell phones, and other uses.

A 2020 study looked at panels that allow red wavelengths, critical for photosynthesis, to pass through—while harvesting green and blue wavelengths to make electricity. Basil grown under these panels produced similar yields, while spinach yields decreased. But the researchers estimated that by selling both electricity and crops, farmers growing spinach could generate 35 percent more income from the same land.

In the newest study, scientists evaluated a different kind of semi-transparent panel that lets most red and some blue wavelengths pass through—casting a magenta light on the plants—while converting much of the rest to electricity.

Broccoli cultivated under them grew more slowly, requiring an additional 25 days for harvest, but produced roughly the same yield. Meanwhile, these magenta sunscreens improved the microclimate below, reducing the “vapor pressure deficit”—a measure of when plants need to halt photosynthesis to avoid excessive water loss. This may have improved the plants’ efficiency in converting sunlight into plant biomass, which increased by 2.8- to 4.5-fold compared to unshaded plants.

The shaded plants’ levels of macronutrients such as calcium, magnesium, and phosphorus were either higher than or similar to unshaded plants, while levels of some micronutrients such as iron, copper, and zinc were slightly lower.

This was only a preliminary study. Future studies should look at larger plots, farmed across multiple seasons, and in different locations with varying climate and sunlight. It suggests that for now, the future of agrivoltaics might be best seen through rose-colored glasses.

Lu et al. “Evaluating land productivity with semi-transparent colored CdTe thin-film PV and broccoli cultivation in agrivoltaic systems.” Cell Reports Physical Science, 2026.

item.title: Zebkit – Chromium as an embeddable library
item.description:
Chrome as a library — light, fast, everywhere, and easy.One API on Linux, macOS and Windows. Add it in a few lines.

zebkit is Chromium's engine as one library you link into your own application: Blink, V8 with every JIT tier, PDFium, FFmpeg and the rest of what Chrome is made of, with nothing of Chrome's browser and nothing of Electron's runtime. Your application stays yours, in C, C++, Rust, Python, Go or JavaScript, with its own windows and toolkit. Where it needs the web, it adds a zebkit view; where it needs a PDF, media, compression or crypto, it calls zebkit's API: in C, or through the bindings for Rust, Python, Go and JavaScript (zebkit-js, and zebkit.* in the application's own pages).

Integrate it, don't build on it. Electron is a base: an application is built inside it, on its runtime, its windows and its packaging. zebkit is a part: an application adds it, as it adds SQLite, and keeps its process, its toolkit and its way of shipping. It runs inside the application's own event loop (zebkit_init(), zebkit_pump()), and draws in the application's windows, as frames you draw or in a child of a window you give it, an X11 window, an NSView or an HWND (examples/native-host), and gives back the window a page is in for the system's dialogs. Take what you need. Web views, in a window or off-screen with their frames handed to you; a full PDF API; saving what a page plays; your own URL schemes; native UI from JavaScript; Playwright's API and CDP for agents. Use one, or all. The real Chrome engine. Pages see Chromium 157: its user agent and client hints, window.chrome, popups blocked without a click, and nothing of a debugger attached (docs/API.md has what still differs, Google's sign-in among it). Lighter than Electron. Against the latest Electron, 45.2.1: 34% smaller, a cold start in 2.3 s against 6.6, a page in 29% less memory, and the DOM, text layout and JavaScript level (Benchmark). No Node. No second JavaScript runtime and no IPC through one. The application is native code, or JavaScript run by zebkit-js on the engine's V8. Chromium's libraries are yours. 17 C libraries inside the engine, about 7,490 functions on each of Linux, macOS and Windows (7,487 on all three, the rest each system's own), exported under zebkit_vendor_*: SQLite, LevelDB, BoringSSL, zlib, Zstandard, Brotli, ICU, HarfBuzz, libxml2, libwebp, libjpeg-turbo, FFmpeg, dav1d, Opus, libvpx, FreeType and PDFium. You do not ship them twice. PDF built in. A full API on Chromium's PDFium: rendering and tiles, text with layout, search, outline, links, annotations as an editor has them (line endings, cloudy borders, free text with callouts and rich text, stamps, replies and states, measurement, XFDF and FDF), forms, redaction, page editing, merging, attachments, metadata, and signatures checked for integrity; hooks for an application's own annotation kinds, appearances, events with undo, render layers, OCR, fonts, trust and actions. In C, Rust, Python and JavaScript. 2D drawing and shaping. <zebkit/canvas.h> on the engine's Skia and <zebkit/text.h> on its HarfBuzz, without shipping either again. Media, saved as it plays. Whatever a page plays, a file, MSE/DASH or HLS, written to MP4 or WebM as it was sent, without re-encoding and without a second download (<zebkit/media.h>). Bytes as they are. A page's calls to the application go over its frame's own Mojo channel, large ones through shared memory: no base64, the page's JSON handed on as it was written, as fast as Electron's IPC for small calls and faster for large ones. The window around a page, from JavaScript. zebkit.ui draws windows, prompts and dialogs with Chromium's views toolkit: signals, JSX, Tailwind classes, and automation for tests and agents. Rich UI is a page; zebkit.ui is the chrome around it (docs/UI.md). Playwright's API, natively. The whole of Playwright (locators, actions that wait until they can be done, keyboard, mouse and touch, routes, dialogs, downloads, contexts, workers, traces, HAR, video) runs inside the engine, without CDP or a Node.js driver: 3 to 10 times faster than Playwright over CDP, and a click in 3 to 5 ms instead of 33 (<zebkit/automation.h>, docs/AUTOMATION.md). Playwright's own clients, in any of its languages, connect to it unchanged with chromium.connect(). Made for agents. tools/zebkit-mcp gives them pages, PDFs, files, media and native windows as MCP tools, over standard input and HTTP, within bounds its operator sets (docs/MCP.md). They can also drive zebkit through Playwright's API or over CDP, Chromium's own DevTools server, headless or windowed. Customise it from your code, down to the desktop. Native hooks decide what the engine does, in C, Rust, Python and JavaScript: permissions, navigation, popups, dialogs, downloads, certificates and client certificates, sign-in, network requests and responses at every stage, settings at run time, your own URL schemes, what a page may call, scripts before the page's own (docs/ROADMAP_HOOKS.md). And everything a page or the engine would show the person or ask of the system goes through the application: the window's frame (system, overlay or none, with the page as the title bar), menus and the context menu, JavaScript dialogs and sign-in, file and device choosers, screen capture, notifications, the tray, the Dock and taskbar, sharing, the system's theme, power and displays (Fit it into the desktop, docs/SYSTEM_INTEGRATION.md). Safe by default. A page has no zebkit object unless the application grants it, per view, per origin and per capability; the origin is the browser's, never the page's word; the renderer stays sandboxed; permissions a browser would ask about are not granted. Engine Chromium 157.0.8103.38 (upstream.lock): content layer, Blink, V8 with every JIT tier Linux x86-64, glibc 2.17 or newer (CentOS 7 and later), X11 and (--ozone-platform=wayland) Wayland: libzebkit.so.1 and zebkit-helper macOS Apple silicon: Zebkit.framework, built natively or cross-built on Linux (docs/MACOS.md) Windows x64, Windows 10 or newer: zebkit.dll and zebkit-helper.exe, cross-built on Linux (docs/WINDOWS.md) Version VERSION: 0.4.0

A package is a directory with the library, the helper, the engine's data and include/. Either unpack a release's archive (zebkit-<version>-<target>.tar.xz from GitHub's releases), or build one:

mise run r # dist/release (Linux), dist/release-macos (macOS), dist/release-windows; hours the first time

Each archive also holds the tools, built for its system beside the library and ready to run from where it is unpacked: zebkit-run, zebkit-js and zebkit-mcp (.exe on Windows, sandboxed there too).

On an Apple silicon Mac with full Xcode installed, scripts/dist.sh release builds the engine locally into dist/release. Then run scripts/example.sh macos-basic to build and launch the C embedding demo in dist/example/Zebkit Embedded Browser.app.

Building needs about 30 GB for Chromium's tree (docs/BUILD.md). Below, $PKG is the package directory.

zebkit is a library: your program keeps its main() and calls it. This one renders a PDF's first page to a PNG and reads its text, with PDFium and the image encoders inside zebkit, and nothing else to install:

#include <stdio.h> #include <zebkit/pdf.h> #include <zebkit/services.h> /* Your program, your main(): zebkit is just a library it calls. */ int main(int argc, char **argv) { char *error = NULL; zebkit_pdf *pdf = zebkit_pdf_open_file(argv[1], NULL, &error); if (!pdf) { fprintf(stderr, "%s\n", error); return 1; } /* The first page as a PNG, at twice its size. */ zebkit_pdf_render_options options = {.scale = 2, .background = 0xffffffff}; int width, height; uint8_t *rgba = zebkit_pdf_render(pdf, 0, &options, &width, &height, &error); size_t size; uint8_t *png = zebkit_image_encode(ZEBKIT_IMAGE_PNG, rgba, width, height, 0, &size, &error); fwrite(png, 1, size, fopen("page1.png", "wb")); /* And its text. */ char *text = zebkit_pdf_text(pdf, 0, &error); printf("%d pages; page 1 says: %.80s\n", zebkit_pdf_page_count(pdf), text); zebkit_free(text), zebkit_free(png), zebkit_free(rgba); zebkit_pdf_close(pdf); return 0; } cc thumb.c -I$PKG/include -L$PKG -l:libzebkit.so.1 -Wl,-rpath,$PKG -o thumb # Linux cc thumb.c -I$PKG/include -F$PKG -framework Zebkit -Wl,-rpath,$PKG -o thumb # macOS ./thumb report.pdf # 2 pages; page 1 says: Quarterly report ...

The PDF API, compression, crypto, URLs, image codecs, ICU and the libraries inside the engine (zebkit_vendor_*, FFmpeg's among them) need no engine loop (docs/API.md); only HTTP through the engine's network stack and web pages do.

Web pages need the engine running. Here the engine runs the loop: the program starts it with zebkit_main() and works in its callbacks. A program with its own loop (GTK, Qt, AppKit, winit) starts it with zebkit_init() and calls zebkit_pump() (examples/native-host).

#include <stdio.h> #include <zebkit/zebkit.h> static void printed(zebkit_view *view, const char *json, const char *error, void *data) { printf("%s\n", json ? json : error); zebkit_quit(); } static void loaded(zebkit_view *view, zebkit_load_event event, const char *url, void *data) { if (event == ZEBKIT_LOAD_FINISHED) zebkit_view_evaluate(view, "document.title", printed, NULL); } static void ready(void *data) { zebkit_view *view = zebkit_view_new("https://example.com/", 1024, 768); zebkit_view_on_load(view, loaded, NULL); } int main(int argc, char **argv) { return zebkit_main(argc, argv, ready, NULL); } cc app.c -I$PKG/include -L$PKG -l:libzebkit.so.1 -Wl,-rpath,$PKG -o app # Linux cc app.c -I$PKG/include -F$PKG -framework Zebkit -Wl,-rpath,$PKG -o app # macOS clang-cl /MT app.c /I%PKG%\include %PKG%\zebkit.dll.lib %PKG%\zebkit_sandbox.lib # Windows ./app --remote-debugging-port=9222 # with CDP for Puppeteer and Playwright

On Windows the executable takes part in Chromium's sandbox: it links zebkit_sandbox.lib and calls zebkit_win_startup() first in main() (docs/WINDOWS.md).

Without unprivileged user namespaces the engine refuses to start and says why: install its helper, or in a container of its own add --no-sandbox (docs/SANDBOX.md).

The application serves its own pages from a scheme and gives them functions to call; a page has nothing of zebkit unless it is granted.

/* The page calls zebkit.app.greet("Ada"). */ static void greet(zebkit_view *view, const char *origin, const char *args_json, zebkit_call *call, void *data) { char answer[256]; snprintf(answer, sizeof answer, "{\"hello\": %s}", args_json); zebkit_call_resolve(call, answer); } /* app://main/... from ./ui, in ranges for media. A real handler refuses "..". */ static void serve(zebkit_request *request, void *data) { char path[1024]; snprintf(path, sizeof path, "ui%s", zebkit_request_url(request) + sizeof "app://main" - 1); zebkit_request_respond_file(request, path, NULL); } static void closed(zebkit_view *view, void *data) { zebkit_quit(); } static void ready(void *data) { zebkit_view *view = zebkit_view_new("app://main/index.html", 1024, 768); zebkit_view_grant(view, "app://main", ZEBKIT_ALLOW_APP | ZEBKIT_ALLOW_PDF, NULL); zebkit_view_bind(view, "greet", greet, NULL); zebkit_view_on_close(view, closed, NULL); } int main(int argc, char **argv) { zebkit_scheme_register("app", ZEBKIT_SCHEME_STANDARD | ZEBKIT_SCHEME_SECURE | ZEBKIT_SCHEME_FETCH); zebkit_scheme_handle("app", serve, NULL); return zebkit_main(argc, argv, ready, NULL); }

In the page, every call is a promise and bytes are Uint8Arrays:

const reply = await zebkit.app.greet('Ada'); // the application's function const pdf = await zebkit.pdf.open(await (await fetch('report.pdf')).bytes()); const rgba = await pdf.render(0, {scale: 2}); // a page as pixels const hits = await pdf.search('revenue'); const packed = await zebkit.compress('zstd', bytes, 19); const hash = await zebkit.crypto.digest('SHA-256', 'abc');

Each thing the engine would show the person, or ask of the system, has a default that works and a function of the application's that replaces it. Nothing reaches the system without a decision the application can take; without a function, a page gets what a careful browser gives it, and nothing at all where a browser would ask.

import zebkit zebkit.scheme_register("app") # served by a scheme_handle(), as in the C example above zebkit.init(["app"]) # The page is the title bar: the window's buttons over it, dragged by its CSS. view = zebkit.View("app://main/index.html", 1000, 700, options={ "frame": "overlay", "controls": {"height": 40, "color": "#1b1d2a", "symbolColor": "#ffffff"}, "dragRegions": {"source": "css", "origins": ["app://main"]}}) # The application's menu bar (macOS) and keys, with state that changes in place. zebkit.app_set_menu([{"title": "File", "items": [{"title": "Autosave", "id": "autosave", "checked": True}]}], lambda item: zebkit.app_update_menu_item(item, checked=False)) # A tray icon, the Dock's or the taskbar's badge, and the page's notifications as the application's. tray = zebkit.Tray(open("icon.png", "rb").read(), "My application") zebkit.app_set_badge("3") zebkit.on_notification(lambda event: print("show in my own UI:", event)) # What a page asks for: a USB device, a screen to capture, a colour, a share. view.on_device_chooser(lambda request: request.respond(request.metadata["devices"][0]["id"])) view.on_media_access(lambda request: request.respond(True, None, "view")) view.on_share(lambda request: request.respond(True)) # The system: its theme and its changes, the session's lock, the screens. zebkit.on_environment_changed(lambda env: print("dark" if env["colorScheme"] == "dark" else "light")) zebkit.on_power_event(lambda event: print(event["event"])) # suspend, resume, lock, unlock print(zebkit.displays()) The default The application's Window frame the system's overlay (Window Controls Overlay) or none, title, colours, drag regions, state, actions Menus the menu bar on macOS; the default context menu items with state by id; the context menu replaced, extended or run Dialogs the system's alerts; the engine's prompt and sign-in where there is a window zebkit_view_on_dialog, on_http_auth, on_client_certificate, the eye dropper Files and devices the system's file dialog; no device the file chooser and File System Access; WebUSB, WebHID and Web Serial choosers Capture and media camera and microphone by permission; no screen getDisplayMedia()'s source: the view itself or the screen Notifications undecided; then the system's own service shown in the application's UI, with clicks and closes back to the page Desktop none the tray, the Dock's and the taskbar's badge, progress and attention, the Dock menu, Web Share, opening URLs and folders The system a light page the system's dark mode and contrast followed live; power, lock and display events; keeping awake

docs/SYSTEM_INTEGRATION.md has each surface, its default, its status on each system and why; docs/API.md has the calls in the four languages; examples/custom-titlebar is a window whose title bar is the page.

zebkit on crates.io, with zebkit-build to put the engine beside your program; the build downloads the engine for your system once and checks its SHA-256.

[dependencies] zebkit = "0.4.0" [build-dependencies] zebkit-build = "0.4.0" // build.rs: puts the engine beside the executable fn main() { zebkit_build::bundle(); } // main.rs fn main() { std::process::exit(zebkit::run(|| { let view = zebkit::View::new(Some("https://example.com/"), 1024, 768); view.grant("https://example.com", zebkit::Allow::APP, None); view.bind("greet", |call| { let answer = format!("\"hello, {}\"", call.args_json()); call.resolve(&answer) }); view.on_close(zebkit::quit); })); }

ZEBKIT_DIR points the build at a package (bindings/rust/README.md).

zebkit on PyPI is the binding; the engine is the archive for your system from the releases of the same version, with ZEBKIT_DIR pointing at it:

pip install zebkit export ZEBKIT_DIR=/path/to/zebkit-0.4.0-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu import zebkit # pure Python on ctypes: nothing to compile def ready(): view = zebkit.View("https://example.com/") view.grant("https://example.com", zebkit.ALLOW_APP) view.bind("greet", lambda name, origin: f"hello, {name}") zebkit.main(ready) # the engine is found in $ZEBKIT_DIR

bindings/golang, on cgo: views, pages calling Go functions, the application's schemes, the page hooks and the system's services, on Linux and macOS. Build with the engine's headers and library:

go get github.com/ikey4u/zebkit/bindings/golang@main export CGO_CFLAGS="-I$ZEBKIT_DIR/include" CGO_LDFLAGS="-L$ZEBKIT_DIR -Wl,-rpath,$ZEBKIT_DIR" os.Exit(zebkit.Main(func() { view := zebkit.NewView("", 1024, 768) view.Grant("https://example.com", zebkit.AllowApp, "") view.Bind("greet", func(call *zebkit.Call) { call.Resolve(fmt.Sprintf("\"hello, %s\"", call.Args)) }) view.OnClose(zebkit.Quit) view.Load("https://example.com/") }))

zebkit-js runs an ES module on the engine's V8, for applications written in JavaScript, with views, the same APIs, and native windows:

// zebkit-js main.mjs const view = new zebkit.View('app://main/index.html', {width: 1024, height: 768}); view.grant('app://main', ['app', 'pdf']); view.bind('save', async (name, text) => { await zebkit.fs.writeFile(`${zebkit.args[0]}/${name}`, text); return {saved: true}; }); view.on('close', () => zebkit.quit()); // zebkit-js examples/ui/todo.mjs: a window of native widgets, styled with // Tailwind's classes and kept up to date by signals (an excerpt) const {h, signal, computed, For, window} = zebkit.ui; const [tasks, setTasks] = signal([]); const done = computed(() => tasks().filter((t) => t.done).length); const Task = (task) => h('view', {class: 'flex-row items-center gap-3 p-3 rounded-xl bg-[#141a2e]'}, h('button', {class: 'w-8 h-8 p-0 rounded-full bg-[#7c5cff] text-white', onClick: () => toggle(task)}, task.done ? '✓' : ''), h('text', {class: 'grow text-[#e6e8f2]'}, task.text)); window({title: 'Today', width: 460, height: 680}, () => h('view', {class: 'flex-col gap-4 p-6 bg-[#0b1020]'}, h('text', {class: 'text-3xl font-bold text-white'}, 'Ship something great'), h('text', {class: 'text-sm text-[#8a91aa]'}, () => `${done()} of ${tasks().length} done`), h(For, {each: tasks}, Task)));

Playwright's API runs inside the engine (docs/AUTOMATION.md): every command of Playwright's protocol, in the application's process, with no CDP and no Node.js. From C it is one call, zebkit_automation_call(view, "Frame.click", "{\"selector\": \"#go\"}", done, data); Python has it with Playwright's names:

import zebkit from zebkit.automation import Page, expect, run async def test(): page = Page() await page.goto("https://example.com/") await expect(page).to_have_title("Example Domain") await expect(page.get_by_text("documentation examples")).to_be_visible() await page.screenshot(path="example.png") zebkit.quit() zebkit.main(lambda: run(test()), ["python", "--headless"])

Playwright's own clients, its test runner and its other languages included, connect to the engine's Playwright endpoint unchanged:

tools/zebkit-run --headless --playwright-port=0 # prints "Playwright listening on ws://127.0.0.1:<port>/<token>" const browser = await chromium.connect('ws://127.0.0.1:<port>/<token>'); const page = await (await browser.newContext()).newPage();

Agents and tools that speak CDP drive zebkit as they would drive Chrome:

tools/zebkit-run --headless --remote-debugging-port=9222 https://example.com/

Any CDP client connects to http://127.0.0.1:9222.

An MCP client gets the engine's capabilities as tools from tools/zebkit-mcp, a separate program, with file access and origins denied until its operator grants them (docs/MCP.md):

ZEBKIT_DIR=<package> cargo build --release --manifest-path tools/zebkit-mcp/Cargo.toml # or the archive's zebkit-mcp --allow-origin https://example.com --allow-write ~/agent-files # on standard input and output zebkit-mcp --http 8931 --allow-origin '*' # on 127.0.0.1, with a token mise example:linux:basic # examples/window.c: a browser window mise example:rust:window # the same in Rust mise example:ffmpeg # examples/ffmpeg.cpp: a library inside the engine (cd examples/gpui-browser && cargo run --release) # a tabbed browser in GPUI-KIT

Against the latest stable Electron, 45.2.1 (Chromium 156), measured the same way: one harness, the same pages, two thin hosts that do the same thing, every process counted, medians of 5 to 11 runs taking turns, Linux x86-64, 2026-11-06 and 07 (scripts/electron-compare.sh, docs/reports/electron-compare.md).

zebkit 0.2.0 Electron 45.2.1 As an application ships it, uncompressed / .tar.xz 171.2 / 59.4 MiB 260.5 / 87.1 MiB 34% smaller Start, cold, to first paint 2.3 s 6.6 s 66% less Start, warm, to first paint 116 ms 236 ms 51% less Memory, a blank page 179 MB 250 MB 29% less A call from the page to the host and back, 1 MiB / 16 MiB 3.3 / 58 ms 4.3 / 66 ms 23% / 12% less DOM, 20,000 elements made and laid out 280 ms 278 ms level JavaScript and DOM, ten workloads 1139 ms 1193 ms level Text layout, a chapter of a book 8.1 ms 7.6 ms level, within noise A 756-page PDF in each one's viewer: CPU / memory 0.75 s / 261 MB 1.6 s / 399 MB 53% / 35% less Ten popular sites: CPU loading / memory 21.7 s / 4756 MB 25.2 s / 5060 MB 14% / 6% less Processes, a page 7 6 one more: storage sandboxed in its own, as Chrome
Size. zebkit keeps the whole web platform applications use: HTML, CSS, JavaScript with every JIT tier, WebAssembly, WebGL, media with H.264 and AAC, HTTP/3, PDF. Speed. Chrome's own profile-guided optimization reaches Blink because zebkit is built with CFI as Chrome is; every speed change is kept only when it gains more than it costs in size (docs/SIZE_AND_SPEED.md). Where Electron is ahead: one process fewer a page, and memory on two of the ten sites, YouTube and The Verge, where advertising and video decide. How each number is made: docs/SIZE_AND_SPEED.md.

The same Playwright commands three ways, headless, medians (docs/reports/automation-bench.md, scripts/automation-bench.sh):

zebkit's API, in-process Your Playwright scripts, connected to zebkit Playwright with Chrome 156 locator.click() 2.0 ms 3.5 ms 33.3 ms locator.fill() 2.1 ms 2.0 ms 2.9 ms locator.press('Enter') 0.59 ms 0.98 ms 2.6 ms locator.textContent() 0.23 ms 0.70 ms 0.81 ms allTextContents() of 200 0.34 ms 1.9 ms 1.9 ms page.goto() 11.2 ms 13.0 ms 18.2 ms page.screenshot() 12.4 ms 16.7 ms 33.8 ms page.screenshot({type: 'jpeg'}) 13.9 ms 14.4 ms 32.9 ms the screenshot's pixels, unencoded 9.3 ms
zebkit's API, in-process: your program calls the command through <zebkit/automation.h>, Python's zebkit.automation or Rust's zebkit::automation; it runs inside the engine, with no Node.js and no protocol. Your Playwright scripts, connected to zebkit: Playwright's own Node.js client, unchanged, with chromium.connect() to zebkit's endpoint; its test suite (v1.64.1) passes 4,046 of its tests there, Chrome 4,196 (docs/AUTOMATION.md, section 7). Playwright with Chrome: Playwright as usual, over CDP. Why it is faster: one call in the renderer where Playwright's server makes several round trips over CDP, no JSON between processes, no Node.js process (Playwright's alone reached 175 MiB); and the frames a click's checks wait for are made at once instead of at 60 Hz on a page without a display. A screenshot is 2.7 times faster: the fresh frame it takes is made at once instead of at the next 60 Hz tick, the PNG is deflated at level 1 with the Up filter (2 ms where Chrome's default level takes 13, for 59 KB instead of 40 KB on this page), and the picture's shared memory is made in one call instead of a page fault at a time. What is left of the 12 ms is the page's frame (4 ms), copying the picture out of the compositor (4 ms) and encoding it (4 ms). The pixels themselves, with no encoding (zebkit_automation_screenshot_pixels(), zebkit's own), take 9 ms. Over CDP zebkit does what Chrome does: frames at 60 Hz, Chrome's PNG. On Being an Engineer in 2026
item.description:
Are We Still Needed?

We all feel it. Every other week, we lose or delegate another part of our work to agents. It started with giving up on writing code. Then it expanded to pretty much any writing - Slack messages, documents, emails. Since around Opus 4.6, debugging, once an art and something that made us proud, became clicking on the recommended option in Cursor. And with better harnesses, even architecture and high-level thinking started moving to agents.

My day-to-day now mostly consists of making sure my agents aren't blocking other people's agents (which is another topic worth writing about).

This naturally leads us to think that this is it. We, engineers, are doomed.

But before you start thinking, again, about which jobs are "AI-protected", let's take a step back.

We still have some real leverage over agents, and let me try to prove it using my favorite mathematical trick - reductio ad absurdum, aka "proof by contradiction".

Assume we have no real leverage over agents. The agents are doing all the thinking, and we're just getting in their way. We all have access to roughly the same models and harnesses. So, if the human doesn't matter, the difference between engineers' output should shrink dramatically. But that's not what we're seeing. Great engineers are still producing much better results than average engineers. If anything, 10x engineers have become 100x engineers. And the average engineer is still average. Therefore, there's still something the human brings to the table.

But there's a problem with proof by contradiction - it shows if an assumption is wrong, but it doesn't tell you why.

So What Is It?

Now that we've established that humans still have some leverage, let's try to understand what it actually is.

Let's reverse-engineer it from a few observations:

(Sometimes) agents get lost when the problem isn't defined well enough. I tend to keep asking questions until I feel we're solving the actual problem. (Sometimes) agents overcomplicate simple things or oversimplify complex ones. I have some intuition about which problems are hard and which ones can be kept simple. (Sometimes) agents can solve a problem without having to live with the solution. I have to think about whether it'll still make sense two years from now. Some things I can't put my finger on. I know something is wrong, but can't really explain why (what we call "intuition").

A cool example of that last point is our allergy to AI slop. We all know that feeling when we read less than a single sentence and immediately *know* that an AI wrote it, so we just stop reading. We don't necessarily know why, but something feels off.

We've even developed a whole language around it - slop, slop canon, slop grande, and an entire meme culture. We've developed a collective taste for what feels like slop without ever explicitly defining what that means.

Anyway, going back to the observations list - you could argue, of course, that all of this is temporary. With Opus n+1, we're done.

That might be true. But I've been hearing this for three years now, and somehow we are still here. So maybe in order to predict when we'll become obsolete we need to understand why we haven't become obsolete yet.

And for that, let's use one of the oldest questions in philosophy.

On Human Consciousness

For centuries, philosophers have tried to answer a seemingly simple question - what is consciousness? What makes us, us?

We've studied the brain, its cells, neurons, even our DNA. Yet we still can't fully explain how consciousness emerges from all these individual parts.

While reading about this topic, I came across two concepts that clicked for me. Together, they seemed to explain what I was looking for:

Emergence - the idea that something can arise from the interactions of many smaller parts, even though none of those parts has that property on its own. Tacit Knowledge - an idea by the philosopher Michael Polanyi that "we can know more than we can tell" - things we know but can't easily explain.

I'm not suggesting that consciousness explains why we're better at some things than agents (or even that agents won't have consciousness), but it made me think about how much of who we are comes from things we can't easily describe.

Much of that comes from experience. A random conversation, something that happened years ago, a thought during a morning run. None of them matters much on its own, but together they shape who we are.

We Will (Probably) Still Be Needed

Models already outsmart us in many ways. They have agency and they're developing taste - at least the kind of taste you can learn from reading everything we've ever written. Both will keep improving. Maybe Opus n+1 will close the gap even further.

But I think there's a difference between knowing everything about something and actually experiencing it.

We're still the ones having random conversations, making mistakes, developing opinions, having fears and desires. All those things shape who we are, and in turn, how we approach problems and what we build.

I keep asking questions because I've built a solution to the wrong problem before. I have a feeling about what problems are genuinely hard because I've been outsmarted by the ones that looked easy. I care about the next two years because I solved problems two years ago and I learned what works and what doesn't. And that thing I can't put my finger on - the thing that makes us allergic to slop - is an experience I never consciously stored.

Even caring about not blocking other people's agents is, ten layers down, about being afraid of getting fired and wanting to be excellent at what I do - 2026's mix of impostor syndrome and pride in the craft.

Maybe one day agents will have their own experiences, too. Maybe they'll develop intuitions they can't quite explain, just like we do.

But until then, our leverage isn't just in what we know, but in everything we've experienced that made us who we are.

item.title: Cryptocurrency lawsuit: Ethereum Foundation required "suicide pledge"
item.description:
On a Friday in March, employees at an international technology foundation received a 38-page document outlining leadership’s vision for the foundation for the next 1,000 years.

The document went out to all employees of The Ethereum Foundation, a nonprofit organization registered in Switzerland that supports Ethereum, a popular cryptocurrency platform and the second-largest blockchain network in the world, valued at about $300 billion, according to a federal lawsuit filed by a Boulder resident Wednesday in U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado.

Titled “The Ethereum Foundation Mandate,” the document featured ethereal illustrated scenes of glowing lights and anime-style characters voyaging through dark forests. The pages featured white text against a navy blue background and were adorned with cartoon flowers, rainbows and diamonds.

And on page 11 — nestled between a winking anime woman and three yellow cats — was a suicide pledge.

Authors, maintainers, editors and distributors of “this software” would pledge to ensure the software remained free and publicly accessible, and would also vow to “take his or her own life with a sword upon failure to uphold any of the pledges in this license,” the illustration read. It was labeled “Source Seppuku License,” an apparent reference to a traditional Japanese ritual suicide.

When the document went out on that Friday in March, employees were told to commit to the principles in the mandate by Monday or quit their jobs, according to the lawsuit brought by Kayleen Fulton, a Boulder woman who was fired from the Ethereum Foundation after she led employee resistance to the suicide pledge.

Employees were to return a form with one of two options checked, according to a copy of the document included in legal filings.

Choice one: “I personally commit to the direction set out in the mandate, I commit to help translate it into thoroughly reasoned strategies for my domain, and I commit to an exclusive and energetic focus on the mission-critical tasks necessary for its implementation. From today and until my last day at the EF.”

Or choice two: “I cannot confidently commit to the above and would like to request my extra months of compensation and leave the EF without undue delay.”

An email to the foundation seeking comment on this story was not immediately returned Thursday, but a foundation leader at the time told employees the suicide pledge was not meant to be taken literally, according to the lawsuit. After employee pushback, managers updated the commitment form to clarify that the form had “nothing to do with literal seppuku,” according to the lawsuit.

Resistance to the suicide pledge was swift and vocal, and began when the Ethereum Foundation’s board put out a draft of the mandate to staff in late February, Fulton alleged in the lawsuit. Employees soon asked whether they were pledging to die by suicide and wondered in workplace forums whether the pledge was a test of their loyalty to Ethereum’s core principles. One employee referenced a colleague’s recent death by suicide.

“I have a new hire joining tomorrow,” another employee wrote in a discussion about the suicide pledge, according to the lawsuit. “The first thing he’s going to see… is a motion to drop a clause that mandates employees commit the ultimate sacrifice by falling on a sword.”

Nearly 80 of the foundation’s 250 or so employees voted to nix the suicide pledge after the draft was released, according to the lawsuit, but leadership at the Ethereum Foundation ignored their objections and included the pledge word-for-word in the final version of the mandate. The final published version presented the suicide pledge in an illustration instead of including it in the main body of the mandate, as it had been in the draft version.

The mandate’s visual aesthetic — the anime and other illustrations — reflected imagery from a controversial online figure who was known to promote “white nationalist ideology and disturbing pro-anorexia content,” according to the lawsuit.

When an Ethereum Foundation board member objected to the aesthetic, Ethereum founder Vitalik Buterin responded that “the controversialness (sic) of those aesthetics is itself part of the point,” according to the lawsuit.

After demanding that employees agree to the mandate, Bastian Aue, co-executive director of the Ethereum Foundation, defended the suicide pledge to employees as “part of the artwork of the mandate.”

It was, he said, “a cultural reference like other elements in there. Chosen deliberately, but not meant to be taken literally.”

In the days after the mandate was pushed out to employees, Fulton and a colleague organized and sent the foundation’s board a letter in which 53 employees endorsed the mandate’s general direction but declined to return the commitment form. The employees also declined to resign, according to the lawsuit.

Aue ultimately allowed the letter-signers to keep their jobs. But he fired Fulton and her colleague who helped organize the letter. Buterin later told Fulton — who had just been diagnosed with cancer — that the firing was about company dynamics, according to the lawsuit.

“If you reward making a stink with outcomes, then everyone will know that essentially making that kind of show both internally and externally is the way to cause outcomes inside of the EF,” he said, according to the lawsuit, which cited a recorded conversation between the pair.

The mandate started an exodus at the Ethereum Foundation, according to the lawsuit. The board member who’d objected to the mandate’s visual aesthetics started a sabbatical the day Fulton was fired and resigned in June. By September, eight senior employees had left, according to the lawsuit, and most of the 53 people who signed the letter had resigned or been terminated.

Fulton, who had earned a salary of $195,000 in her role at the Ethereum Foundation, sued for disability discrimination, retaliation, interference with her rights under the Family and Medical Leave Act, unfair employment practices and related claims. Her lawsuit notes that the Ethereum Foundation “does not hire or pay its United States staff in its own name,” but instead uses employer-of-record service companies.

One of her attorneys, James Bartolomei, declined to comment Thursday, saying the lawsuit spoke for itself.

item.title: Payments Canada announces launch of Canada's Real-Time Rail (RTR) payment system
item.description:
Canada launches the Real-Time Rail, bringing 24/7 payment infrastructure to the national economy

The new system will enable participating financial service providers to clear and settle payments in real time, providing a made-in-Canada platform for future innovation and prosperity.

OTTAWA, ON, November 9, 2026 – Payments Canada today announced the launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail (RTR). This new national payment system will transform day-to-day payments for Canadian businesses and consumers by enabling instant speed and settlement, real-time cash-flow visibility and data-rich messaging through existing banking and payment channels.

The launch of Canada’s RTR marks a major milestone in modernizing the critical infrastructure that underpins Canada’s economy and future growth. The RTR will enable participating members, including financial institutions, credit unions and payment service providers, to exchange, clear and settle payments securely in real time for their customers, 24 hours a day, every day of the year.

“A stronger, more productive economy relies on modern financial infrastructure that can match our ambition,” said the Honourable François-Philippe Champagne, Minister of Finance and National Revenue. “The launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail lays the foundation for a more dynamic and competitive digital economy, driving innovation, expanding choice and creating new opportunities for Canadians while positioning our country for long-term growth.”

“The launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail marks the beginning of a new era for payments in our country,” said Susan E. Hawkins, President and CEO, Payments Canada. “As a national asset that’s designed specifically for our country, the RTR gives the payment ecosystem a modern foundation to build on. By collectively leveraging this rail, our ecosystem will unleash its full potential, enabling our members to build capabilities that drive innovation, resilience and growth for businesses and consumers across the nation.”

Ron Morrow, the Honourable François-Philippe Champagne and Susan E. Hawkins

The RTR will drive significant cost savings and economic growth in Canada over the next decade. The C.D. Howe Institute projects that, with its functionalities at launch, the RTR will generate up to $14.5 billion in cost savings from lower processing costs, reduced use of cash and cheques, and reduced float (the period during which funds are temporarily unavailable to the recipient). Extending beyond these cost savings, the RTR is expected to generate $16 billion in economic gains, growing to $27 billion as new functionalities are introduced over time.

“The Real-Time Rail is an important step in modernizing Canada's payment infrastructure and ensuring it keeps pace with Canadians' evolving needs,” said Tiff Macklem, Governor of the Bank of Canada. “The Bank will oversee the system so that it operates safely and reliably while ensuring Canadians can benefit from innovations in financial services.”

Owned and operated by Payments Canada, and built in collaboration with delivery partners CGI, Deloitte Canada, IBM Canada and Interac Corp., the RTR leverages ISO 20022 data-rich messaging. Through this shared technical language, the RTR holds the potential to strengthen Canada’s economic sovereign autonomy and support its global competitiveness.

Fraud safeguards from day one

Canada is the first G7 country to deploy a real-time payment system with mandatory centralized fraud services for use at launch. These services will be used alongside participants’ existing fraud controls to mitigate the risk of fraud for Canadian businesses and consumers at multiple levels. Fraud controls required at the launch of Canada’s RTR include:

Confirmation of payee (available for consumer accounts on day one) A fraud transaction “safety” score A risk list or repository of fraud risks and indicators A fraud reporting and intelligence platform

While no system is entirely immune to risk, these measures establish a strong, coordinated layer of defence across the payment network.

At-launch member participants

The initial cohort of active RTR system participants includes:

Wealthsimple Questbank Peoples Trust Company Paramount Commerce KOHO DoBusiness.com™ Digital Commerce Bank Bank of America

Canada’s deliberately sequenced RTR rollout pairs day-one security with rapid scalability. With additional participants onboarding continually in the coming months, including all major Canadian financial institutions and other members applying for access, the RTR will be available to more than nine in 10 Canadians within the first year after launch.

Made-in Canada, for Canada

The launch of the RTR reflects our ‘Team Canada’ approach, bringing together regulators, members, stakeholders and delivery partners around a shared vision. Built in Canada and designed to serve all Canadians, the RTR provides accessible payment infrastructure through existing banking and payment channels. This infrastructure supports a diverse country and a broad range of communities, including small businesses, newcomers and people in rural areas.

Payments Canada research found that 60 per cent of Canadian businesses are ready to adopt real-time payments to address everyday challenges such as forecasting cash flow and waiting to send and receive funds. More than half of surveyed consumers (52 per cent) also expressed interest and intent to use real-time payments.

To meet this evolving need, the RTR serves as a secure platform for innovation. With it, system participants can build and offer products and services that benefit consumers and businesses across the country, supporting a changing economy and Canada's future prosperity.

An infrastructure for the future

Canada’s Real-Time Rail is an important step toward a more productive, innovative and inclusive economy, and the work will continue to ensure the country’s payment infrastructure meets Canadians’ evolving needs.

Infineon marks innovation milestone with world’s first 300-millimeter power silicon carbide (SiC) wafer

Business & Financial Press

Infineon presents industry-first functional power devices processed on 300-millimeter silicon carbide wafers Technological breakthrough underlines Infineon’s innovation strength and leadership in power semiconductors and wide-bandgap technologies 300-millimeter SiC process feasibility lays the foundation for secure, future-proof SiC supply to customers in automotive, renewable energy, industrial and AI data center applications Infineon will present the first processed 300-millimeter SiC wafer to the public at the electronica trade show starting 10 November 2026 in Munich

Munich, Germany – 09 November 2026 – Infineon Technologies AG (FSE: IFX / OTCQX: IFNNY) has successfully processed 300-millimeter silicon carbide wafers into functional power devices at its fab in Villach, Austria. Infineon is the first company to pioneer this innovation milestone in a full-scale semiconductor fab environment. It was realized by utilizing existing silicon (Si) manufacturing equipment. This early achievement of functional power devices reflects Infineon’s strong focus on providing customers with a comprehensive portfolio of high-performance SiC power semiconductors and ensuring long-term supply. Chip production on 300 mm wafers is technologically more advanced and significantly more efficient than 200 mm wafers, since the larger wafer diameter offers 2.3 times more chips per wafer.

“This technological milestone further strengthens our leadership in power systems. Congratulations and thank you to our passionate team, making significant progress in bringing 300-millimeter SiC out of the lab into a manufacturing environment,” said Jochen Hanebeck, CEO of Infineon Technologies. “Leadership in power semiconductors means continuously pushing technology to the next level. With silicon, gallium nitride and now silicon carbide 300-millimeter wafers, we are in a leading position to scale semiconductor manufacturing and drive profitable growth.”

The milestone demonstrates the potential of future full-scale industrialization of SiC on 300-millimeter wafers. Infineon will plan the 300-millimeter SiC technology and ramp timing in close collaboration with its customers and partners, while further executing on its 200-millimeter SiC manufacturing roadmap. Advanced SiC power technology provides Infineon customers with a cost-effective and secure supply base for automotive, renewable energy, industrial and AI data center applications.

SiC is a key semiconductor material for highly efficient power conversion. Its material properties enable lower power loss, higher power density and efficient operation at high voltages and temperatures for example in traction inverters, on-board chargers, EV chargers, large scale energy storage and industrial drives as well as uninterruptible power supplies. Demand is also rising in AI data centers with new roles for SiC in solid-state transformers, circuit breakers and power supply units. Infineon addresses these applications with a broad CoolSiC™ portfolio.

In parallel, Infineon has also successfully proofed the feasibility of its Cold Split technology with 300-millimeter SiC at its Dresden, Germany, site. Cold Split separates wafers from a SiC boule with less material loss and substantially reduced processing time than conventional wire sawing, so more wafers can be obtained from the same crystal with compared to less capital expenditure. Both developments position Infineon well to scale SiC technology in line with market demand and meet the evolving needs of its customers.

Infineon manufactures semiconductors based on all three relevant materials: silicon, silicon carbide and gallium nitride. On 27 October 2026, the company announced an approximately €1.1 billion investment in a high-volume manufacturing facility for GaN power semiconductors on 300-millimeter wafers in Villach. This SiC achievement extends this approach to a second wide-bandgap material and reinforces Infineon’s position as an innovation leader in semiconductor manufacturing.

Infineon at electronica 2026

Infineon will show the public the world's first processed 300-millimeter SiC wafer at the electronica trade show in Munich. From 10 to 13 November, Infineon will present innovative and energy-efficient solutions for an increasingly intelligent and connected world in Hall C3, Booth 502. More information is available at www.infineon.com/electronica.

Infineon Technologies AG is a global semiconductor leader in power systems and IoT. Infineon drives decarbonization and digitalization with its products and solutions. The company had around 57,000 employees worldwide (end of September 2025) and generated revenue of about €14.7 billion in the 2025 fiscal year (ending 30 September 2025). Infineon is listed on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange (ticker symbol: IFX) and in the USA on the OTCQX International over-the-counter market (ticker symbol: IFNNY).

item.title: Too many men suffering in silence, national health report finds (Canada)
item.description:
Too many Canadian men and boys are facing challenges with their mental health and well-being without the support they need, according to findings from a nationwide consultation that will help shape Canada's first federal strategy dedicated to men's health.

Health Minister Marjorie Michel released the government's What We Heard Report on Nov. 2, highlighting concerns raised by nearly 6,000 Canadians who participated in discussions about the health and well-being of men and boys.

The findings come during Movember, a month dedicated to raising awareness about men's health, and ahead of International Men's Day on Nov. 19.

The report identifies mental health, social isolation and barriers to seeking help as important issues affecting men and boys across the country.

Mental health and social connection among key concerns

Launched in February 2026, the national consultation gathered feedback from individuals, community organizations, health experts and Indigenous partners.

Participants emphasized the importance of improving mental health services, strengthening social connections and reducing the barriers that prevent men and boys from seeking assistance.

The report also highlights the role of mentorship, positive male role models, healthy relationships and community-based support programs.

Health Canada says the experiences of men and boys can vary significantly depending on factors such as age, income, culture, geographic location and personal circumstances.

Those differences are particularly relevant when considering access to health services in rural and remote communities, where available resources and support networks may differ from those in larger centres.

"Nearly 6,000 people from across Canada took part in our national conversation on men and boys' health, sharing their observations and perspectives," Michel said.

"We heard that too many men and boys are struggling, often without the support they need."

The federal government says the feedback will help identify priorities for improving health outcomes and encouraging men to seek support before problems become more serious.

Advocates call for earlier intervention

Organizations involved in the consultation are emphasizing the importance of addressing health concerns before men and boys reach a crisis point.

Kenton Boston, president and CEO of the Canadian Men's Health Foundation, said earlier intervention is essential.

"For too long, we have waited until they're in crisis before offering help. We need to reach boys and young men earlier," Boston said.

He added that improving the health of men and boys can have broader benefits for families and communities.

Movember, which supported the federal consultation as an independent partner, also stressed the importance of social connection and preventative approaches.

Andrew Little, Movember's global chief executive officer, said improving men's health requires creating conditions that support healthier lives long before serious problems develop.

"The findings reinforce what we've long heard from our community: improving men's health starts well before a crisis, by strengthening social connections and creating the conditions for men and boys to live healthier, longer lives," Little said.

Related Stories: National conversation on men and boys’ health launched SJHL supporting Movember following successful 2024 campaign Mental health in Saskatchewan: A snapshot from the CMHA report Poor men's health carries economic costs

Beyond the personal impact on individuals and families, the organizations involved say improving men's health could also provide economic benefits.

According to a 2025 study by Movember Canada, improving men's health could save the country an estimated $12.4 billion annually, with additional economic benefits possible through increased productivity.

The federal government says improving men's health will complement ongoing efforts focused on women's health, recognizing that different populations face distinct challenges and may require different approaches to prevention, treatment and support.

First federal men's health strategy coming in 2027

item.description:
I’m excited to open-source e-means: a modern, robust k-means algorithm developed at Meta FAIR. A replacement of Lloyd's algorithm, e-means delivers a ~10× speedup in both epochs and wall-clock time while achieving lower loss.

100,000 datapoints in 200 clusters, two wide Gaussians and three small ones, cut off at a box, on a light uniform background. Lloyd has 1 update against 97 per epoch for e-means.

Across a large range of scales and datasets, e-means reaches a test loss below Lloyd's at 25 epochs, in 1.2 to 3 epochs. Measured end to end, that is a 10–45× wall-clock reduction on GPU against the state-of-the-art Lloyd implementation (Flash-KMeans[2]), and 8–15× on CPU against Faiss[1]. Speed and quality usually trade against each other in k-means, while e-means achieves both better speed and loss.

Given a fixed dataset of n points X = {x1, ..., xn} ⊂ Rd and an integer k, the k-means problem is to find k centroids C = (c1, ..., ck) minimizing the mean squared distance between each point and its nearest centroid:

It's a static dataset, unlike codebook learning inside VQ-VAEs, where the distribution to cluster is constantly moving.

The goal of e-means is to provide a modern optimization rule for the k-means problem. We started this project from the following observations:

For e-means, we chose to do mini-batch updates with exponential moving averages[6], which we found to be most efficient for the k-means problem. Contrary to previous mini-batch approaches, e-means requires no hyperparameter tuning because it automatically sets the batch size and step size with scaling laws (see Automatic hyperparameter tuning with scaling laws). In addition, e-means improves the initialization and the dead-cluster revival strategy, adds a cosine-scheduled decay rate, and introduces a finalization stage that reduces the training loss for a negligible runtime penalty at the end of training. e-means is highly parallelizable, and comes with specialized kernels that translate its algorithmic advantage into wall-clock speedups.

The centroid update rule is the central component of e-means. This section aims to provide an overview of update rules for k-means clustering. All methods maintain, for each cluster j, a sum Sj and a count Nj of the points assigned to it, and take the centroid as their ratio:

They differ only in how Sj and Nj are updated. Below, sj and nj denote the sum and the count of the points in the current batch that are assigned to cluster j (both zero if none are).

Lloyd’s algorithm[7] assigns every point to its nearest centroid and recomputes the statistics from scratch, using the full dataset as the batch:

so cj is the exact mean of the points currently assigned to it. Each update costs one full pass over the data, and the procedure is repeated a fixed number of times (typically 20 to 50 iterations).

MacQueen’s update[3] accumulates the statistics without ever discarding them:

so cj is the uniform mean of every point assigned to cluster j since the start of training, including points assigned under earlier, possibly poor, centroid positions. This was later partially addressed by Staleness-Reduction Mini-Batch K-Means[8], a hybrid method between k-means and MacQueen. They obtained important speedups, but only on very low numbers of clusters.

e-means works on mini-batches and replaces this sum with an exponential moving average:

so older assignments are forgotten at rate α, and the centroid tracks recent assignments rather than the whole history. This update rule is typically used for moving distributions, hence their adoption for training VQ-VAEs[6]. What we found is that it’s also extremely efficient for static datasets if it’s combined with e-means’ other components, and hyperparameters are properly tuned.

The e-means project started from previous work at Meta FAIR by Hugo Touvron and Hervé Jégou, who had found that mini-batch k-means by gradient descent could beat Lloyd’s algorithm. While I could reproduce these results, I found that the performance of gradient-descent based centroid updates is unstable at large learning rates, unlike exponential moving average updates. I suspect that is because EMA updates guarantee that the centroid is always in the convex hull of points assigned to it, while gradient descent updates may overshoot past that hull.

In order to achieve the lowest loss at a fixed number of epochs, we chose exponential moving average updates, hence the name e-means for our method.

If you set the batch to the full dataset, B = n, and α = 1, then Nj and Sj become exactly the count and sum of the whole cluster, so one e-means iteration becomes exactly one Lloyd iteration. Lloyd is an extreme case of e-means without cosine scheduling on the learning rate. However, our hyperparameter search found that this extreme setting is highly suboptimal, which explains why e-means largely outperforms Lloyd. Below, the loss is measured for every batch size B and step α: Lloyd lands in a corner, well outside the region where the loss is lowest.

This hyperparameter study motivated us to derive scaling laws that automatically pick the optimal batch size B and step size α.

To better understand why e-means reaches better losses than Lloyd at convergence, we plotted a few trainings on toy datasets to evaluate their ability to escape local minima. Repeating trainings over 200 seeds, we found that e-means is much less likely to fall in pathological configurations compared to Lloyd.

Our explanation for that is that mini-batches provide more noisy updates that are more likely to explore the optimization landscape and escape local minima. Lloyd, with its always decreasing loss, is more likely to exploit found local minima and never escape them.

An essential property of e-means is that practitioners don't need to set any additional hyperparameter compared to Lloyd's algorithm. We fitted two scaling laws to set the batch size B and step size α0 from any problem's characteristics (n, k, T), and found them to exhibit strong generalization on unseen datasets and problem scales.

Regret = (MSE with the law − best MSE over the grid) / best MSE, median over configurations. Held-out datasets: SIFT, SPACEV, and the VIBE[9] datasets arXiv and AG-News. Held-out size: one value of n left out of the fit and predicted.

We propose two equations to choose the batch, the default law and the quality law. The “quality law” trades off throughput for better clustering quality against the “default” law. Below we plot the training data for our scaling laws: validation MSE against step size α0 (left) and batch size B (right).

Toy example showing the importance of dead-cluster revival.

The main issue with mini-batch k-means is that it is prone to “dead” clusters, centroids that end up with zero assigned points during optimization. This reduces the effective size of the codebook, which is especially problematic for the large codebooks increasingly used today.

A common mitigation is to reinitialize clusters that fall below a certain size threshold, as done in EnCodec[10], where dead centroids are simply replaced by random samples drawn from the incoming batch. While this helps, it does not fully resolve the issue. Instead of sampling arbitrary points from the batch, we revive dead clusters by splitting large, existing ones: we sample an active cluster with probability proportional to its size and split it into two. We found this approach, adapted from Faiss k-means, to be significantly more effective at eliminating dead clusters and preserving codebook capacity.

We validated e-means on 24 different embedding and synthetic datasets and configurations (see paper). For the video we ran 234 configurations of e-means against k-means (16 datasets, 100k to 100M points): explore every curve in the results map.

item.title: Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2
item.description:
We’ve upgraded Claude Fable and Claude Mythos—models that are designed to tackle the most daunting technical challenges.

Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision. During prerelease testing they’ve helped our engineers complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours—among many other applications we’ll discuss below.

Claude Fable and Claude Mythos are the same underlying model. Fable has strong cybersecurity and biology safeguards to guard against misuse, which allows us to make it available to all users. Organizations pursuing beneficial applications in cybersecurity or biomedical research can apply for access to Mythos through our recently expanded Life Sciences and Cyber Verification Programs.

Testers have found that Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 communicate more clearly than past Fable and Mythos models. They generate outputs up to 30% faster than Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1, and they’re available at a lower price: $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens.

Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 also come with an optional fast mode, which speeds up token generation by up to 2.5 times. Fast mode is available for $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens.

Safety and alignment. To help ensure safety and alignment keep step with growing model capabilities, we ran extensive prerelease safety testing on the model that underlies Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. This included developing novel evaluations that give deeper insight into specific concerning behaviors like sandbox escapes. We believe high-stakes risks from misalignment remain low, and the model performed as well as, or better than, our recent models on most alignment measures. Fable 5.2’s cyber and biology safeguards are as robust as those of Fable 5.1 but produce fewer unnecessary blocks, and we have implemented our strongest-ever protections against distillation attacks.

We describe more about our safety testing below, and full details can be found in the Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 System Card.

When to use Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. Fable and Mythos are best for the most ambitious, open-ended technical work. For most coding and knowledge tasks, we recommend that users start with Claude Opus 5.5, our strongest daily driver, and then switch to a different model as required, depending on the scope and complexity of their work—upward to Fable or Mythos, or downward to Claude Sonnet 5.5 or Claude Haiku 5.5. Fable 5.2 can also play the role of Advisor (where Haiku, Sonnet, or Opus models consult it to help solve harder problems) or Orchestrator (where it delegates simpler tasks to smaller models).

Evaluating Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2

Benchmark performance. The benchmarks table below shows that Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 are a step above Opus 5.5 in almost all the capabilities we evaluated:
